question.text:
An 8-year-old boy presents with knee pain and joint effusion. Biopsy and staging studies reveal a distal femoral osteosarcoma with contamination of the knee joint. Which treatment option offers the best local control and optimal functional outcome for this patient?
Answer Choices: (A) Rotationplasty (B) Modified Van Nes rotationplasty with ankle fusion (C) Arthrodesis with intercalary allograft (D) Wide local excision with vascularized fibular graft (E) Intra-articular resection with expandable prosthesis (F) Below knee amputation with custom prosthesis (G) Above knee amputation (H) Segmental resection with distraction osteogenesis (I) Limb-sparing surgery with allograft reconstruction (J) Extra-articular resection, endoprosthetic reconstruction, and free flap coverage

options.B: Modified Van Nes rotationplasty with ankle fusion
options.D: Wide local excision with vascularized fibular graft
options.F: Below knee amputation with custom prosthesis
options.J: Extra-articular resection, endoprosthetic reconstruction, and free flap coverage

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The patient has osteosarcoma with joint contamination, indicating a high risk of recurrence and functional impairment. Limb-sparing surgery with allograft reconstruction offers the best chance for local control and functional outcome by preserving the limb while addressing the tumor and joint involvement. Other options like amputation or extensive resection with reconstruction may result in significant functional deficits.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: Rotationplasty and amputation are considered for limb salvage, but the presence of joint contamination makes them less favorable. Arthrodesis is not ideal for a young patient with a limb-sparing goal. While wide local excision with a graft is a reasonable option, it may not provide adequate local control in the presence of joint contamination. Intra-articular resection with an expandable prosthesis is not a standard approach for osteosarcoma. Segmental resection with distraction osteogenesis is not typically used for osteosarcoma. Extra-articular resection with endoprosthetic reconstruction and free flap coverage is a complex procedure that may not be necessary in this case.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient has a distal femoral osteosarcoma with knee joint contamination, indicating a high-risk osteosarcoma requiring aggressive treatment. Limb-sparing surgery with allograft reconstruction (I) offers the best balance of local control and functional outcome by preserving the limb while providing structural support through allograft reconstruction. This approach avoids the complications of amputation and provides better quality of life for a pediatric patient.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: Distal femoral osteosarcoma with knee joint contamination
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Considered amputation options (F, G) but ruled them out due to the young age and the potential for limb-sparing. Extra-articular resection (J) was considered but ruled out due to the joint contamination. Rotationplasty (A) and modified Van Nes (B) were considered but ruled out due to their complexity and less favorable functional outcomes compared to allograft reconstruction.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient has distal femoral osteosarcoma with joint contamination, requiring complete resection of the tumor and joint to ensure local control. Limb-sparing options (I, D) are less ideal due to joint involvement. Amputation (F, G) is less optimal for functional outcomes in children. Option J provides extra-articular resection, endoprosthetic reconstruction, and free flap coverage — ensuring tumor-free margins, structural integrity, and soft tissue coverage, which is critical for local control and functional recovery in pediatric patients.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Contamination of the knee joint necessitates extra-articular resection to ensure complete tumor removal and prevent local recurrence.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Rotationplasty (A, B) and amputation (F, G) were considered but are inferior for functional outcomes in children. Arthrodesis (C) and allograft reconstruction (I) may be insufficient for joint contamination. Endoprosthetic reconstruction with free flap coverage (J) is superior for achieving both oncologic control and functional restoration.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Arthrodesis (C), wide local excision with graft (D, J), and amputation (F, G) were considered but are inferior in terms of preserving limb function and achieving local control compared to rotationplasty.
